questions.prompt: A sound source moves directly towards a stationary observer. State how the observed frequency compares with the source frequency and name the denominator sign used in the moving-source Doppler expression.
Which statement describes every electromagnetic wave?

options.A: It is longitudinal and requires a material medium.
options.B: It is transverse and can travel through free space.
options.C: It is transverse only when its frequency is high.
options.D: It travels through free space by vibrating air particles.

questions.prompt: Two electromagnetic waves have different frequencies while travelling in free space. Which quantity is the same for both?
The frequency of an electromagnetic wave in free space is doubled. What happens to its wavelength and speed?

options.A: Wavelength halves and speed stays constant.
options.B: Wavelength doubles and speed stays constant.
options.C: Wavelength stays constant and speed doubles.

questions.prompt: An electromagnetic signal travels through free space with frequency $6.00\times10^{10}$ Hz. Use $c=3.00\times10^8$ m s$^{-1}$.

parts.prompt: Calculate the wavelength of the signal.
Explain why increasing the signal frequency does not increase its speed in free space.

questions.prompt: A transmitter sends two electromagnetic pulses P and Q across a free-space distance of $9.00\times10^7$ m. P has frequency $1.50\times10^9$ Hz and Q has frequency $6.00\times10^{14}$ Hz.

figure.purpose: Make the common free-space path and two different frequencies clear without revealing wavelength or travel-time results.
figure.brief: Original Cambridge-inspired black-and-white line diagram. Show one transmitter at left and one receiver at right separated by 9.00 x 10^7 m. Draw two parallel pulse paths labelled P, 1.50 x 10^9 Hz and Q, 6.00 x 10^14 Hz. Do not show wave-region names, wavelengths, speed values or arrival order.
figure.alt_text: Two electromagnetic pulses of different frequencies travel along equal free-space paths from one transmitter to one receiver.

parts.prompt: Determine whether either pulse arrives first and calculate the travel time.

questions.prompt: A detector in free space records the electric-field variation of an electromagnetic pulse. Successive peaks on the time trace are separated by $2.50\times10^{-9}$ s. Use $c=3.00\times10^8$ m s$^{-1}$.

figure.purpose: Require extraction of period from a field-time trace before applying the free-space wave equation.
figure.brief: Original Cambridge-inspired black-and-white line graph. Vertical axis electric field E and horizontal axis time t. Draw a sinusoidal trace with two adjacent peaks and a horizontal bracket labelled 2.50 x 10^-9 s. Add a separate rightward energy-transfer arrow beside the graph. Do not label period, frequency, wavelength or answers.
figure.alt_text: An electric-field time trace has adjacent peaks separated by two point five times ten to the minus nine seconds.

parts.prompt: Calculate the frequency of the pulse.
Calculate its wavelength in free space.
State what makes this wave transverse and explain why the plotted up-and-down field variation does not mean that the pulse travels up and down.
